H1.text: A pin on a map. A seat number in an exam hall. A treasure map saying ten steps east, five north.

H2.text: Three different things, all answering one question. Where exactly is it?

H3.text: Aarav parked his bicycle somewhere in the big college ground. His friend asks, where is it?

H4.text: Aarav points and says, over there. But how far? And which way?

H5.text: Physics answers both with just one arrow. By the end of this video, you will draw it yourself.

P1.text: So what is a position vector?

P2.text: First, pick one fixed point to measure from, the origin O. Here, the college gate.

P3.text: Next, draw two axes. The x axis points east. The y axis points north.

P4.text: Now draw an arrow from the origin straight to the bicycle. That arrow is the position vector, r.

P5.text: Its length tells you how far. Its direction tells you which way. Both answers in one arrow.

P6.text: Using i hat and j hat, r equals x i hat plus y j hat. Here, twenty i hat plus ten j hat metres.

S1.text: Now watch it live. Aarav rides from P to Q along a curved path.

S2.text: At P, he is twenty metres east and ten metres north of the gate.

S3.text: As he rides, the position arrow swings and stretches, always from O to the bicycle.

S4.text: Watch the graph. x grows steadily. y climbs fast, then levels off.

S5.text: Slow motion. Freeze. Right now, r is the arrow from O to the bicycle, at this instant.

S6.text: He stops at Q, fifty metres east and fifty north.

S7.text: Now the big idea. Draw one arrow straight from P to Q. This is the displacement, delta r.

S8.text: The road curved. But the displacement is one straight arrow, from start to finish.

D1.text: Let's find delta r from the two position arrows, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. The position at the start is r one. The position at the end is r two.

D3.text: Step two. O to P, then P to Q, gets you to Q. So r one plus delta r equals r two.

D4.text: Step three. Move r one across. Delta r equals r two minus r one. Final minus initial.

D5.text: Step four. In parts, delta r equals delta x i hat plus delta y j hat.

T1.text: Remember this. Displacement is the final position minus the initial position.

R1.text: Now a surprising question. What if we pick a different origin?

R2.text: On the left, the origin is the gate. On the right, it is the canteen.

R3.text: From the canteen, r one is a new arrow. r two is a new arrow too.

R4.text: But both arrows changed by the same extra piece, the arrow from the canteen to the gate.

R5.text: When we subtract, that extra piece cancels out.

R6.text: So, pause and think. With the origin at the canteen, does delta r change, or stay the same?

R7.text: It stays the same! Thirty i hat plus forty j hat from both. Position depends on the origin. Displacement does not.

K1.text: Side by side. A position vector starts at the origin and ends at the object. Move the origin, and it changes.

K2.text: A displacement starts where the motion starts and ends where it ends. It ignores the origin and the path.

K3.text: Now you try. Aarav rides a full loop and parks exactly where he started. What is his displacement? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Zero! He ended where he began, so r two minus r one is zero. The loop's length is distance, not displacement.

W2.text: A ball moves from A, one comma two, to B, six comma fourteen, in metres. Find its displacement.

W3.text: Delta x equals six minus one. Five metres.

W4.text: Delta y equals fourteen minus two. Twelve metres.

W5.text: So delta r equals five i hat plus twelve j hat metres.

W6.text: Its size is the root of five squared plus twelve squared. Root one sixty nine. Thirteen metres.

W7.text: Direction: tan theta is twelve over five, so theta is about sixty seven degrees.

X2.text: Many students subtract the wrong way round, and write delta r as r one minus r two.

X3.text: That arrow points backwards, from the end to the start. Always final minus initial. r two minus r one.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As a quick calculation: find the displacement from two position vectors, and its size.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A particle moves from r one to r two along a curved path ten metres long. What is the magnitude of its displacement? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Seven metres.

A2.text: Delta r is r two minus r one, which is two i hat, minus six j hat, plus three k hat.

A3.text: Its size is the square root of four plus thirty six plus nine. The square root of forty nine. Seven.

A4.text: Ten is the path length, the distance. Eleven adds parts without squaring. Two point one just subtracts the sizes. All traps.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why do we need an origin before we can write a position vector?

Y3.text: Two. Why does moving the origin not change the displacement?

Y4.text: Three. Can displacement be zero when distance is not? Give an example.

N1.text: Next time: one slanted arrow hides two straight arrows. We find them in vector components in two dimensions.
